full_judgment:
23. Mr. Mahmood submits that in the present case there is absolute violation and non-observance of the provisions of section 105C of the Companies Act. The materials on record prima facie show that the Board of Directors did not convene any meeting and issue any further shares to the existing share-holders for the alleged enhanced 1,51,000 shares. Further, no notice was given to the existing share-holders inviting their attention as to whether they would accept it or not. On this point Mr. Mahmood has referred to several decisions as reported in AER (1935) 456; AIR 1950 (SC), 172; AIR 1953 (SC), 385; AIR 1949 (Born.), 56; AIR 162 (Urissha) 202 and 1920 (I) Chancery Division, 77. In the decision reported in 1935 AER 456 their lordships in interpreting the Companies Act and powers and functions of the directors, held as follows: 

 24. In the case reported in AIR 1950 (SC) 172 it is held by their lordships that this section 105C is intended to cover a case where the directors decide to increase by issuing further shares within the authorized limit, for it is only within that limit that the directors, can decide to issue further shares, unless they are precluded from doing even that by the regulations of the Company. Therefore, the section becomes applicable only when the directors decide to increase capital within the authorized limit by the issue of further shares. From this decision it appears that within the authorized limit of share-capital the directors are competent to issue the shares amongst the share-holders as required under section 105C of the Companies Act. In the case reported in AIR 1949 (Born) 56 it is held by their lordships of the Division Bench that in deciding to issue new shares the directors are exercising fiduciary powers, and they should exercise those powers in the interest of and for the benefit of the Company of which they are the directors. If they exercised this merely for the purpose of maintaining their own control or retaining their own majority, then the Court would interfere and prevent the issue of new shares on the ground that the directors were guilty of a breach of faith towards the company of which they were the directors, But, if it was once established that the company was in need of additional funds and that the fresh issue was decided upon in order to make good those funds, then, whatever other motives might have actuated the directors, the Court will not interfere with the discretion exercised by the directors, From this decision it also appears that this increase of new shares and the distribution of the same is absolutely within the domain of the directors.
